newsitem.title: USA: N. Korea delays peace talks until Saturday.
newsitem.headline: N. Korea delays peace talks until Saturday.

text.p: North Korean negotiators delayed resuming talks with the United States and South Korea on a landmark peace proposal all day on Friday, forcing officials to reschedule the talks for Saturday.

The crucial talks, adjourned after an inconclusive day-long meeting on Wednesday, were to resume on Friday morning. But six hours after the planned 10 a.m. (1400 GMT) start, U.S. officials said they had been told by the North Korean delegation it was still awaiting direction from Pyongyang.
After waiting all day, the U.S. side announced late in the afternoon that the talks had been rescheduled for 10 a.m. (1400 GMT) on Saturday.

The South Korean delegation had planned to leave New York for Seoul on Friday night. But late in the day, a senior member, Yu Myung-hwan, director general of the foreign ministry's North American affairs bureau, said the team was willing to stay through Saturday.
"Still I have some hope that we can strike a deal by tomorrow," Yu told reporters.
Another South Korean official expressed frustration with the delay, saying "this is not a game." He said he was "suspicious" of North Korea's claim to be consulting with Pyongyang.

The meeting was called to hear Pyongyang's formal response to a year-old U.S.-South Korean proposal for four-party peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War by replacing the fraying armistice with a peace treaty.
China would also participate in the peace negotiations.

A spokesman for North Korea's mission to the United Nations, who declined to be identified, told Reuters after his country's team failed to arrive for the Friday morning session on time: "We need to contact with capitals."
Asked if there was a problem, he said: "I cannot say anything in connection with that."
A day earlier, U.S. officials said Pyongyang could not expect new food aid donations from Washington or Seoul before providing a conclusive answer on the peace talks proposal.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, speaking in Washington, denied this might be a reason for North Korea's postponement of the Friday talks.

He shrugged off the delay, saying "This kind of thing happens all the time in negotiations." Burns declined to predict how long the meeting might go and also suggested it might carry over into Saturday.
U.S. officials have said privately that Pyongyang essentially accepted the peace talks proposal in Wednesday's talks but then conditioned its acceptance with demands for additional food assistance.

The three delegations opened Wednesday's meeting with optimistic statements and an apparent warmth and conviviality. Later, they all reported progress and said they hoped to settle the issue when they resumed on Friday.
But Pyongyang's Stalinist regime has been preoccupied with increasingly severe food shortages caused by two years of floods, insisting on more and more internatonal help.

U.S. officials have said Pyongyang cannot expect a massive effort to deal with its food problems until it enters peace talks and begins to defuse tensions on the volatile and heavily armed Korean peninsula.
After some scepticism in Washington and elsewhere, it has been widely accepted that North Korea is facing serious food shortages that are likely to reach famine stage in the next two months.
North Korea and independent experts say the country needs 2.3 million tons of food this year.
The U.N. World Food Programme recently appealed for 200,000 metric tons of food, with Washington offering one-quarter of that amount, including a $15 million contribution on Monday.
